blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights two dystopian scenarios from the 'Re-coding Black Mirror' workshop papers, exploring the social and ethical implications of pervasive technology. The first paper, 'Shut up and run: the never-ending quest for social fitness,' examines the negative consequences of wearable sensors and social media data in health insurance, mortgages, and social ranking systems. The paper presents three scenarios (Alice, Bob, Charlie) where individuals face discrimination, social pressure, and health penalties based on data-driven assessments, leading to loss of privacy, free will, and even mental health issues like orthosomnia. The author emphasizes the need for government intervention to prevent such discriminatory practices. The second paper, 'May I have your attention please? Building a dystopian attention economy,' draws parallels from the Black Mirror episode 'Fifteen Million Merits' to current advertising trends, where attention is commodified. The paper argues that advertisers increasingly prioritize attention over information, and speculates on the feasibility of implementing ad-skipping payment systems, including blockchain-based solutions, in the near future.
paper_title: Shut up and run: the never-ending quest for social fitness
paper_abstract: —We analyze prior work in social cybersecurity and present a structuring of this literature based on its pertinence to four S&P-relevant social behaviors: (1) negotiating access to shared resources, (2) shared and social authentication, (3) managing self-presentation, and (4) influencing others’ S&P behaviors. We further break down these domains into four scales of social distance—intimate, personal, social, and public— showing that desired access control policies, authentication methods, and privacy and sharing preferences vary across these social scales. We evaluate the current landscape of work through the lens of Ackerman’s social-technical gap in social computing systems, finding that while social behaviors clearly impact S&P preferences and needs, existing S&P systems are designed with little understanding of these behaviors. This mismatch forces users to choose between implementing their ideal S&P policies or reducing social friction. To address this mismatch, we outline a research agenda for social cybersecurity work that better aligns S&P goals with social needs, preferences and behaviors. I. I NTRODUCTION Many end-user cybersecurity and privacy (S&P) behaviors are inherently social: we share information with other people in our social networks [1], we ask questions of friends and family about best S&P practices when confused [2], [3], and we coordinate with and help others to be safe online [4]. Indeed, work in usable S&P has alluded to the existence of social influences in S&P behaviors as early as the late 1990s [5]. Yet, most tools aimed at helping end-users improve their security and privacy have been designed primarily with individual behaviors in mind. As examples, there has been a vast amount of work focused on improving the usability of individual authentication systems [6] and access control policy interfaces [7] [8], or increasing individual users’ comprehension of S&P warnings [9].
